etymologies.etymologyHTML: Borrowed into Middle English trespas, from Old French trespas (“passage; offense against the law”), from trespasser.

definitions.definition: (law) An intentional interference with another's property or person.

quote.citation: 2019 December 18, Andrew Roden, “New measurements reveal improvement in punctuality”, in Rail, page 24:
quote.text: External infrastructure issues such as severe weather and trespass caused 17.1% of [train] cancellations, [...].

Network Rail has produced a free downloadable comic highlighting the consequences of railway trespass. Between March 23 and April 26, there were 1,024 trespass incidents on the railway. [...] it is based on the company's award-winning safety film 18, which shows the dangers of trespass, especially around electrified lines.

quote.citation: 1611, The Holy Bible, […] (King James Version), London:  […]  Robert Barker, […], →OCLC, Matthew 6:14–15:
quote.text: Forgive us our trespasses, as we forgive those who trespass against us

etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English trespassen, borrowed from Old French trespasser (“to go across or over, transgress”), from tres- (“across, over”) + passer (“to pass”).

definitions.definition: (intransitive, now rare) To commit an offence; to sin.

quote.citation: 1611, The Holy Bible, […] (King James Version), London:  […]  Robert Barker, […], →OCLC, 2 Chronicles 28:22:
quote.text: In the time of his distress did he trespass yet more against the Lord.

definitions.definition: (transitive, obsolete) To offend against, to wrong (someone).

quote.citation: 1526, [William Tyndale, transl.], The Newe Testamẽt […] (Tyndale Bible), [Worms, Germany: Peter Schöffer], →OCLC, Matthew vj:[14]:
quote.text: And forgeve us oure trespases, even as we forgeve them which trespas us.

definitions.definition: (intransitive) To go too far; to put someone to inconvenience by demand or importunity; to intrude.

quote.citation: 1813 January 27, [Jane Austen], Pride and Prejudice: […], volume (please specify |volume=I to III), London:  […]  [George Sidney] for T[homas] Egerton, […], →OCLC:
quote.text: "Indeed I have, sir," was her answer. "She is a great deal too ill to be moved. Mr. Jones says we must not think of moving her. We must trespass a little longer on your kindness."

definitions.definition: (law) To enter someone else's property illegally.
(obsolete) To pass beyond a limit or boundary; hence, to depart; to go.

quote.citation: 1523–1525, Jean Froissart, John Bourchier, 2nd Baron Berners (translator), Froissart's Chronicles
quote.text: Soon after this, noble Robert de Bruce  […]  trespassed out of this uncertain world.

definitions.definition: (transitive, law enforcement) To decree that a person shall be arrested for trespassing if he or she returns to someone else's land.

quote.citation: 1996 April 16, Glenn Campbell, “Another Business Office Found”, in The Groom Lake Desert Rat‎[1], number 35, Rachel, NV, archived from the original on 23 February 1998:
quote.text: "You were trespassing on private property when you were taking pictures," he said, with no hint of courtesy. "I must trespass you. Come with me."

quote.citation: 2012 June 21, Greg O'Connor, “Criminal trespasses police officers”, in Stuff‎[2]:
quote.text: The entire police force has in effect been trespassed from a Wellington property to stop officers checking whether a heavy-sleeping offender is complying with an overnight bail curfew.
